title: Divide & Conquer: Quick Sort Algorithm
subject: DAA
aim: To implement and analyze the time complexity of Quick Sort algorithm using the Divide and Conquer strategy.
theory:
Quick Sort is an efficient sorting algorithm based on the Divide and Conquer approach. It selects an element as a 'pivot' and partitions the array into two sub-arrays according to whether elements are less than or greater than the pivot. The sub-arrays are then sorted recursively.

Key Concepts:
1. Pivot Selection: Strategies include picking the first element, last element, median, or a random element.
2. Partitioning: Rearranging the array such that all elements less than the pivot are on the left and greater on the right.
3. Recursion: Applying Quick Sort to the left and right sub-arrays.

Time Complexity:
- Best Case: O(n log n) - occurs when pivot divides array into roughly equal halves.
- Average Case: O(n log n)
- Worst Case: O(n^2) - occurs when the array is already sorted or reverse sorted.

Space Complexity: O(log n) auxiliary space due to recursion stack.
procedure: Select a pivot element from the array (commonly the last element).
Initialize two pointers: i (boundary of elements smaller than pivot) and j (current scanner).
Scan through elements from index low to high - 1 using pointer j.
If element at j is smaller than or equal to pivot, increment i and swap element at i with element at j.
Place pivot element in its correct position by swapping element at i + 1 with pivot.
Return the pivot position (partition index).
Recursively apply Quick Sort to the left subarray (low to pIndex - 1) and right subarray (pIndex + 1 to high).

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
Which algorithmic paradigm does Quick Sort follow?

assignment.defaultCode:
def quick_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    pivot = arr[len(arr) // 2]
    left = [x for x in arr if x < pivot]
    middle = [x for x in arr if x == pivot]
    right = [x for x in arr if x > pivot]
    return quick_sort(left) + middle + quick_sort(right)

# Test array
numbers = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
print('Sorted:', quick_sort(numbers))

result: The Quick Sort algorithm was successfully implemented. Array elements were sorted in ascending order. Empirical time analysis verified O(n log n) average performance on random inputs.
conclusion: Quick Sort is a highly practical in-place sorting algorithm with low overhead. Choosing a randomized pivot effectively avoids the worst-case O(n^2) runtime.

title: Dynamic Programming: 0/1 Knapsack Problem
subject: DAA
aim: To formulate and solve the 0/1 Knapsack Problem using Dynamic Programming technique and evaluate space-time tradeoffs.
theory:
The 0/1 Knapsack Problem is a combinatorial optimization problem. Given a set of items, each with a weight and a value, determine the number of each item to include in a collection so that the total weight is less than or equal to a given limit and the total value is as large as possible.

In 0/1 Knapsack, items cannot be broken into smaller pieces (either take an item completely or leave it).

Dynamic Programming Approach:
We build a 2D table DP[i][w] representing the maximum value attainable using a subset of first i items with a weight capacity w.

Recurrence Relation:
DP[i][w] = max(DP[i-1][w], value[i-1] + DP[i-1][w - weight[i-1]]) if weight[i-1] <= w
else DP[i-1][w]
procedure: Define inputs: weights array, values array, capacity W, and number of items n.
Create a DP table of dimensions (n + 1) x (W + 1) initialized to 0.
Iterate i from 1 to n (items) and w from 1 to W (capacity).
For each item, if item weight is less than or equal to current capacity w, decide whether to include it or exclude it by picking the maximum value.
Otherwise, exclude the item: DP[i][w] = DP[i-1][w].
The value in DP[n][W] represents the maximum achievable profit.
Backtrack from DP[n][W] to trace which specific items were selected.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of 0/1 Knapsack using Dynamic Programming?

result: The 0/1 Knapsack solution yielded the optimal profit for given capacity constraints, overcoming exponential brute-force complexity by reusing optimal subproblems in O(n * W) time.
conclusion: Dynamic programming eliminates redundant computation in 0/1 Knapsack by storing subproblem solutions, demonstrating the power of optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

title: Greedy Method: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
subject: DAA
aim: To compute single-source shortest paths in a weighted directed/undirected graph with non-negative edge weights using Dijkstra's algorithm.
theory:
Dijkstra's Algorithm finds the shortest distance from a single source node to all other nodes in a graph with non-negative edge weights.

Greedy Strategy:
At each step, it selects the unvisited node with the minimum distance metric, updates distances to its adjacent neighbors (relaxation step), and marks the selected node as processed.
procedure: Initialize distance to source node as 0 and all other nodes as infinity.
Maintain a set of unvisited nodes.
Find unvisited node u with the smallest tentative distance.
For node u, iterate over all adjacent unvisited neighbors v.
Relax edge (u, v): if distance[u] + weight(u, v) < distance[v], update distance[v].
Mark node u as visited.
Repeat until all reachable nodes are visited.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm cannot be guaranteed to work correctly with which type of edges?

result: Dijkstra's algorithm accurately generated shortest path trees from source node A to all graph destinations in O((V + E) log V) time using min-priority queues.
conclusion: Dijkstra's algorithm is optimal for non-negative edge weights. For graphs with negative edge weights, Bellman-Ford must be used instead.
